course.title: SOC Fundamentals
course.description: A practical analyst-first course that develops the foundations needed to work in a security operations center. Students learn how SOCs operate, how to collect and evaluate security telemetry, investigate identity/endpoint/network alerts, write and test detections, use MITRE ATT&CK and threat intelligence for context, perform hypothesis-driven hunts, document and respond to incidents, operate runbooks and automation safely, and measure detection and response quality. The course is designed for serious beginners who want a transferable SOC skill set rather than training tied to one vendor platform.
prerequisites: Basic understanding of computer operating systems and files.
Basic networking concepts such as IP addresses, ports, DNS, and client/server communication.
Comfort using a command-line terminal; familiarity with both Linux and Windows is helpful.
Basic reading of JSON and plain-text log records.
No prior SOC or security-operations job experience is required.
learningOutcomes: Explain the mission, roles, workflows, escalation paths, and operating model of a SOC.
Identify high-value identity, endpoint, network, cloud, and application telemetry and evaluate data quality.
Interpret timestamps, structured events, syslog, JSONL, DNS, HTTP/TLS, process, and network records in investigations.
Use SIEM-style search workflows and write basic KQL queries for security analysis.
Design, test, tune, and document behavior-focused detections using Sigma-style logic and MITRE ATT&CK mapping.
Triage and investigate authentication, phishing, endpoint, and network security alerts using evidence from multiple data sources.
Apply incident-response concepts for classification, containment, evidence preservation, recovery, communications, and improvement.
Use threat-intelligence concepts, STIX/TAXII, and ATT&CK as contextual inputs without treating indicators as proof of compromise.
Conduct a hypothesis-driven threat hunt using baselines, outliers, Zeek-style network telemetry, and Suricata EVE JSON concepts.
Design safe SOC automation, runbooks, metrics, and controls that keep monitoring and response trustworthy.
Complete an end-to-end synthetic SOC investigation that produces a reproducible case, detection improvement, and telemetry improvement.

modules.title: SOC Mission and Operating Model
modules.description: Build the mental model for how a SOC works as an operational capability: roles, queues, risk, escalation, and shift continuity.

lessons.title: What a SOC Does
lessons.description: A security operations center (SOC) is a capability for continuous security monitoring, analysis, coordination, and response. This lesson separates the SOC mission from the tools used to achieve it and introduces the analyst’s core loop: collect evidence, detect signals, validate, scope, respond, document, and improve.
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and boundaries of a SOC.
Describe the analyst workflow from signal to closure.
Distinguish a security capability from a product such as a SIEM or EDR.

notes.text: A SOC is not synonymous with a SIEM. A SIEM is one technology that centralizes and analyzes telemetry; the SOC also depends on people, processes, data sources, decision criteria, escalation paths, and feedback loops.

items: Core loop: visibility → detection → triage → investigation → response → recovery/lessons learned.
Every alert is a hypothesis to test, not proof of compromise.
The SOC must optimize for risk reduction and useful decisions, not alert volume.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes a SOC?
options: A dashboard that stores firewall logs
A capability combining people, process, telemetry, analysis, and response
quiz.answer: A capability combining people, process, telemetry, analysis, and response
quiz.explanation: A SOC is an operational capability; tools such as SIEM and EDR support it but do not define it.

summary: Core loop: visibility → detection → triage → investigation → response → recovery/lessons learned.
Every alert is a hypothesis to test, not proof of compromise.
The SOC must optimize for risk reduction and useful decisions, not alert volume.

lessons.title: SOC Roles, Tiers, and Escalation
lessons.description: Analysts need clear ownership. This lesson introduces common SOC roles without treating tier numbers as universal standards: alert monitoring and triage, deeper investigation and detection engineering, incident response, threat hunting, and security engineering. The emphasis is on responsibility and escalation criteria rather than job-title labels.
learningObjectives: Map common SOC responsibilities to operational stages.
Define escalation triggers using impact, confidence, and scope.
Explain why tier labels vary between organizations.

items: Tier names are organizational conventions; responsibilities matter more than numbers.
Escalate on potential business impact, uncertainty, spread, privileged access, persistence, or evidence destruction.
Record handoff context: what happened, what was checked, what is known, what is unknown, and what action is requested.

quiz.question: Which is the strongest reason to escalate an alert quickly?
options: The alert has a colorful dashboard widget
The alert may involve privileged access and active compromise
The alert arrived during a quiet shift
The alert uses a new logo
quiz.answer: The alert may involve privileged access and active compromise
quiz.explanation: Potential high impact, active compromise, and privileged access increase urgency and justify escalation.

summary: Tier names are organizational conventions; responsibilities matter more than numbers.
Escalate on potential business impact, uncertainty, spread, privileged access, persistence, or evidence destruction.
Record handoff context: what happened, what was checked, what is known, what is unknown, and what action is requested.

lessons.title: SOC Operating Models and Shift Handover
lessons.description: A 24×7 SOC succeeds only when context survives shift changes. This lesson covers queue ownership, severity states, evidence links, handover notes, and minimizing duplicate work. It also introduces the idea of an operational runbook as a decision aid rather than a rigid substitute for judgment.
learningObjectives: Design a shift handover that preserves investigation context.
Use severity and status consistently in case management.
Explain what a runbook should and should not automate.

items: Case/alert identifier and severity.
Observed behavior and affected identities/assets.
Queries and evidence reviewed, with timestamps.
Containment actions already taken and actions still pending.
Clear next action and owner.

quiz.question: What makes a handover useful?
options: A complete context record plus a clear next action
quiz.answer: A complete context record plus a clear next action
quiz.explanation: Handover value comes from preserving context, evidence, status, ownership, and next steps.

summary: A 24×7 SOC succeeds only when context survives shift changes. This lesson covers queue ownership, severity states, evidence links, handover notes, and minimizing duplicate work. It also introduces the idea of an operational runbook as a decision aid rather than a rigid substitute for judgment.

lessons.title: Risk, Severity, and Analyst Decision Making
lessons.description: SOC triage is a risk decision under uncertainty. This lesson introduces impact, likelihood/confidence, asset criticality, identity privilege, and scope as separate dimensions. Students learn why a high-signal event can still be low risk and why a weak signal can deserve urgent review when context is severe.
learningObjectives: Separate technical confidence from business impact.
Prioritize cases using explicit evidence-based criteria.
Document uncertainty instead of hiding it behind a severity label.

items: Severity is not the same as confidence: you may be highly confident that an event occurred but uncertain whether it was malicious.
Asset criticality and identity privilege can raise priority without changing the underlying detection logic.
Good case notes state assumptions and unknowns explicitly.

quiz.question: Which factor is independent from detection confidence?
quiz.answer: Business impact
quiz.explanation: Business impact is a risk dimension separate from whether the analyst is confident the detected event occurred.

summary: Severity is not the same as confidence: you may be highly confident that an event occurred but uncertain whether it was malicious.
Asset criticality and identity privilege can raise priority without changing the underlying detection logic.
Good case notes state assumptions and unknowns explicitly.

tasks.title: Build a SOC Escalation Matrix
tasks.description: Create a small severity/escalation matrix for common SOC events.
tasks.problemStatement: Your team needs consistent decisions for suspicious login bursts, endpoint malware alerts, exposed administrative services, and confirmed account takeover.
objectives: Define impact and confidence criteria.
Specify escalation owners and target response states.
Document what evidence must accompany escalation.
tasks.hint: Separate event confidence from business impact and define at least one example in each severity band.
tasks.solutionCode:
# Example decision table
levels = {
    "low": {"impact": "limited", "action": "queue for routine review"},
    "medium": {"impact": "material", "action": "analyst investigation and owner notification"},
    "high": {"impact": "significant", "action": "immediate escalation and containment review"},
}
print(levels)
tasks.solutionExplanation: The table keeps severity tied to business impact and expected handling rather than to a tool-specific label. A production matrix would also include confidence, asset criticality, privilege, and evidence requirements.

modules.title: Security Telemetry and Logging
modules.description: Teach the evidence foundation of SOC work: log sources, timestamps, normalization, collection, retention, and protection.

lessons.title: Security Telemetry and Evidence
lessons.description: SOC analysis depends on telemetry that is timely, sufficiently detailed, trustworthy, and searchable. This lesson defines events, alerts, evidence, telemetry, and context, then explains why a single log line rarely proves an incident by itself.
learningObjectives: Differentiate raw events, alerts, and evidence.
Identify the context needed to interpret a security event.
Explain why data quality affects detection quality.

items: An event is an observation; an alert is a rule- or model-generated signal; evidence is information used to support an analytical conclusion.
Useful context often includes time, identity, host, source/destination, action, outcome, and process or application details.
Telemetry must be treated according to its trust level: it can be missing, delayed, duplicated, or tampered with.

quiz.question: Why is context essential to SOC telemetry?
options: It allows an analyst to interpret whether an event is meaningful
It guarantees every alert is malicious
It eliminates the need for investigation
quiz.answer: It allows an analyst to interpret whether an event is meaningful
quiz.explanation: Context connects an event to identities, assets, time, actions, and surrounding activity.

summary: An event is an observation; an alert is a rule- or model-generated signal; evidence is information used to support an analytical conclusion.
Useful context often includes time, identity, host, source/destination, action, outcome, and process or application details.
Telemetry must be treated according to its trust level: it can be missing, delayed, duplicated, or tampered with.

lessons.title: Log Sources: Identity, Endpoint, Network, Cloud, and Application
lessons.description: A useful SOC collects complementary views of an environment. This lesson covers identity/authentication events, endpoint process and file telemetry, network metadata, cloud control-plane logs, and application logs. Students learn which questions each source can answer and where blind spots arise.
learningObjectives: Match investigation questions to appropriate log sources.
Identify likely blind spots when a key source is absent.
Explain why application logs add context that infrastructure logs may lack.

items: Identity logs answer who authenticated, from where, with what outcome, and sometimes what was attempted afterward.
Endpoint telemetry exposes process execution, parent-child relationships, file activity, services, and persistence-related changes when enabled.
Network telemetry provides communication context; it may not reveal encrypted content.
Cloud audit logs capture control-plane actions that may never appear on traditional network devices.
Application logs can carry business context unavailable to OS and network logs.

quiz.question: Which source is most directly useful for determining who performed a cloud administrative action?
quiz.answer: Cloud control-plane audit logs
quiz.explanation: Cloud audit logs record administrative and API activity in the service control plane.

summary: Identity logs answer who authenticated, from where, with what outcome, and sometimes what was attempted afterward.
Endpoint telemetry exposes process execution, parent-child relationships, file activity, services, and persistence-related changes when enabled.
Network telemetry provides communication context; it may not reveal encrypted content.
Cloud audit logs capture control-plane actions that may never appear on traditional network devices.
Application logs can carry business context unavailable to OS and network logs.

lessons.title: Time, Timestamps, and Synchronization
lessons.description: Timeline reconstruction fails when clocks disagree. This lesson covers event time versus ingestion time, time zones, clock drift, ordering uncertainty, and the operational importance of synchronized time sources. Students build a habit of preserving original timestamps and normalizing carefully.
learningObjectives: Distinguish event time from collection or ingestion time.
Normalize timestamps without losing their original representation.
Explain how clock drift can distort an incident timeline.

notes.text: Never overwrite the source timestamp without preserving it. Analysts may need both event time and ingestion time to explain delayed or reordered records.

items: Use UTC or an explicitly documented normalized representation for cross-system analysis.
Clock synchronization is a foundational investigative dependency, not a cosmetic configuration.

quiz.question: Why retain both event time and ingestion time?
options: To distinguish when an activity happened from when the collector received it
quiz.answer: To distinguish when an activity happened from when the collector received it
quiz.explanation: The two timestamps support accurate timelines and explain collection delays.

summary: Use UTC or an explicitly documented normalized representation for cross-system analysis.
Clock synchronization is a foundational investigative dependency, not a cosmetic configuration.

lessons.title: Syslog, JSON, and Structured Events
lessons.description: Security data becomes easier to search and correlate when fields are structured consistently. This lesson contrasts classic syslog framing with structured JSON event records and highlights message parsing, field naming, severity, facility, transport, and vendor-specific extensions.
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose of syslog and structured event formats.
Parse a simple structured event into searchable fields.
Describe why schema consistency matters for correlation.

notes.text: <34>1 2026-09-07T13:42:15Z host-a sshd[812]: Failed password for user "analyst" from 198.51.100.23 port 51122

items: RFC 5424 defines a layered syslog protocol and structured message format.
Structured JSON is convenient for machine processing but still requires consistent field meaning and validation.

practicals.title: Parse and Normalize Sample Security Logs
practicals.description: Convert a small mixed log sample into a normalized JSONL format so analysts can filter by common fields.
steps: Create a text file containing three syslog-like events and three JSON events.
Write a Python parser that emits normalized records with timestamp, host, event_type, user, and src_ip where available.
Preserve the original line in an `raw_event` field.
Print the normalized records as JSON Lines.
Check that events with missing optional fields remain parseable.
practicals.solution:
import json
from datetime import datetime


def normalize(record):
    return {
        "ts": record.get("ts"),
        "host": record.get("host"),
        "event_type": record.get("event_type", record.get("event")),
        "user": record.get("user"),
        "src_ip": record.get("src_ip"),
        "raw_event": record["raw_event"],
    }

# Example JSONL input records can be loaded and normalized with
# json.loads(line) and normalize(...), while raw syslog-like lines
# can be mapped to the same output shape by a dedicated parser.
print(json.dumps(normalize({
    "ts": "2026-09-07T13:42:15Z",
    "host": "host-a",
    "event": "authentication_failure",
    "user": "analyst",
    "src_ip": "198.51.100.23",
    "raw_event": "example"
}), indent=2))
practicals.output: The student should produce JSON Lines records sharing the same core fields while preserving the original event. Missing values remain null rather than being silently invented.

quiz.question: What is the main SOC advantage of structured event fields?
options: They support consistent search and correlation
They prevent attackers from creating logs
quiz.answer: They support consistent search and correlation
quiz.explanation: Fielded data enables queries, joins, aggregation, and normalized detection logic.

summary: RFC 5424 defines a layered syslog protocol and structured message format.
Structured JSON is convenient for machine processing but still requires consistent field meaning and validation.

lessons.title: Log Collection, Retention, and Protection
lessons.description: Centralized collection improves search and correlation, but log pipelines themselves become security and reliability targets. This lesson covers source coverage, collection paths, buffering, retention, storage capacity, access control, tamper protection, and deletion policies.
learningObjectives: Design a basic collection and retention policy.
Identify availability and integrity risks in a logging pipeline.
Explain why access to security logs must itself be monitored.

items: CIS Control 8 emphasizes collection, review, retention, adequate storage, and standardized time synchronization.
CISA recommends enabling logging on relevant servers, firewalls, endpoints, and cloud services and centralizing logs where practical.
OWASP recommends protecting logs against unauthorized access, modification, and deletion and monitoring logging health.

quiz.question: Why protect logs from unauthorized deletion?
options: Logs are only useful for compliance
Deletion can remove evidence needed for detection and incident response
quiz.answer: Deletion can remove evidence needed for detection and incident response
quiz.explanation: Attack investigation often depends on historical records; tampering or deletion can undermine analysis.

summary: CIS Control 8 emphasizes collection, review, retention, adequate storage, and standardized time synchronization.
CISA recommends enabling logging on relevant servers, firewalls, endpoints, and cloud services and centralizing logs where practical.
OWASP recommends protecting logs against unauthorized access, modification, and deletion and monitoring logging health.

tasks.title: Design a High-Value Log Source Plan
tasks.description: Create a prioritized log-source plan for a small enterprise SOC.
tasks.problemStatement: The organization can only onboard a limited number of sources during the first phase. Choose sources that support identity compromise, endpoint execution, network communication, and cloud administration investigations.
objectives: Prioritize sources by investigation value.
Record what each source can and cannot prove.
Define a minimum retention and protection requirement.
tasks.hint: Start from investigation questions rather than products: who authenticated, what executed, where it communicated, and which administrative changes occurred.
tasks.solutionCode:
sources = [
    ("identity", "authentication and privilege events", "account compromise"),
    ("endpoint", "process/file/service telemetry", "execution and persistence"),
    ("network", "DNS/flow/firewall metadata", "communication and scope"),
    ("cloud", "control-plane audit events", "administrative changes"),
    ("application", "user/business security events", "application-layer context"),
]
for name, coverage, use_case in sources:
    print(f"{name}: {coverage} -> {use_case}")
tasks.solutionExplanation: The solution starts from investigative questions and assigns a source capable of answering each question. A production plan should also capture owners, collection method, latency, volume, retention, and access controls.

modules.title: Network and Endpoint Foundations for SOC
modules.description: Give analysts enough networking, DNS, web, process, and cross-platform event knowledge to investigate without becoming dependent on a single tool.

lessons.title: TCP/IP and Ports for SOC Analysts
lessons.description: SOC analysts do not need to become network engineers, but they must reason about addresses, ports, protocols, sessions, and directionality. This lesson gives the minimum networking model needed to interpret firewall, flow, IDS, proxy, and DNS events.
learningObjectives: Interpret source/destination IPs and ports.
Explain the difference between TCP connection state and application protocol.
Use network directionality when evaluating suspicious connections.

items: A destination port identifies a service endpoint, not proof of what software is actually listening.
Direction matters: outbound from a workstation to a rare external service has a different meaning from inbound traffic to a public server.
Private addresses, NAT, proxies, and load balancers can obscure the original client identity.

quiz.question: What does a destination port tell an analyst?
options: The intended or observed service endpoint number
quiz.answer: The intended or observed service endpoint number
quiz.explanation: A port number helps identify the service endpoint but does not prove the application or intent.

summary: A destination port identifies a service endpoint, not proof of what software is actually listening.
Direction matters: outbound from a workstation to a rare external service has a different meaning from inbound traffic to a public server.
Private addresses, NAT, proxies, and load balancers can obscure the original client identity.

lessons.title: DNS as Security Telemetry
lessons.description: DNS is an unusually valuable SOC signal because many applications rely on it before making network connections. This lesson covers query/response structure, record types, caching, TTL, NXDOMAIN, unusual domains, and why DNS alone should not be treated as proof of malicious intent.
learningObjectives: Interpret common DNS security fields.
Recognize useful anomaly dimensions such as rarity and query bursts.
Correlate DNS findings with endpoint and network evidence.

notes.text:
# Example Zeek dns.log-style fields
query=cdn.example.test
qtype_name=A
rcode_name=NOERROR
answers=203.0.113.55

items: Look at who queried, what was queried, when, how often, and whether the answer changed.
Rare domains can be legitimate, so analyst confidence rises when DNS is corroborated by process, endpoint, or network behavior.

practicals.title: Correlate DNS and Connection Metadata
practicals.description: Use synthetic DNS and connection JSON records to identify hosts that queried a rare domain and then established an outbound connection.
steps: Create a JSONL file containing DNS and network_connection events.
Group DNS queries by host and domain.
Join matching hosts to subsequent connections within five minutes.
Output the host, domain, destination IP, and timestamps.
Write one fact and one hypothesis for the result.
practicals.output: A matched host/domain/destination set with timestamps. The student should explicitly note that correlation increases context but does not prove malicious intent.

quiz.question: Which is a stronger DNS investigation method?
options: Correlate unusual DNS with the requesting host and subsequent connection behavior
Ignore DNS because it is normal traffic
quiz.answer: Correlate unusual DNS with the requesting host and subsequent connection behavior
quiz.explanation: Rarity is a useful signal, but context and corroboration determine whether it is meaningful.

summary: Look at who queried, what was queried, when, how often, and whether the answer changed.
Rare domains can be legitimate, so analyst confidence rises when DNS is corroborated by process, endpoint, or network behavior.

lessons.title: HTTP, TLS, and Proxies in Investigation
lessons.description: Analysts frequently see web traffic through proxies, TLS metadata, or partial HTTP logs. This lesson teaches what HTTP logs can reveal, what encrypted TLS hides, and how proxies and inspection points change the available evidence. Students learn to avoid overclaiming from a single network record.
learningObjectives: Identify common HTTP request fields useful in investigation.
Explain what TLS encryption changes for visibility.
Use proxy context when attributing web activity to an endpoint.

items: HTTP telemetry can expose methods, hosts, URIs, user agents, response codes, and timing when visible to the sensor.
HTTPS encryption protects application payloads from on-path observers unless an authorized inspection point exposes additional fields.
Proxy logs can be more useful for user attribution than raw NAT gateway logs because they may carry identity and request context.

quiz.question: What is a safe conclusion from ordinary TLS metadata?
options: The connection was encrypted and metadata may still support attribution or anomaly analysis
The exact URL path is always visible
quiz.answer: The connection was encrypted and metadata may still support attribution or anomaly analysis
quiz.explanation: TLS metadata can support timing, endpoint, certificate, and connection analysis without exposing encrypted content.

summary: HTTP telemetry can expose methods, hosts, URIs, user agents, response codes, and timing when visible to the sensor.
HTTPS encryption protects application payloads from on-path observers unless an authorized inspection point exposes additional fields.
Proxy logs can be more useful for user attribution than raw NAT gateway logs because they may carry identity and request context.

lessons.title: Endpoint Processes and Parent-Child Relationships
lessons.description: Process trees are central to endpoint investigation. This lesson introduces executable names, command lines, parent/child processes, user context, integrity levels, services, and persistence. The emphasis is on behavioral reasoning: unusual parent-child combinations, unexpected paths, and execution under unusual identities.
learningObjectives: Read a simple process tree.
Explain why parent-child relationships provide investigative context.
Identify suspicious process characteristics without declaring guilt from a single field.

items: A process name alone is weak evidence; combine path, signer, parent, command line, user, frequency, and network behavior.
Benign administrative activity can resemble attacker behavior, so analyst triage must consider expected software and role.

quiz.question: Why is parent-child process context valuable?
options: It shows how a process was launched and provides behavioral context
quiz.answer: It shows how a process was launched and provides behavioral context
quiz.explanation: Process lineage helps analysts understand execution chains and unusual behavior.

summary: A process name alone is weak evidence; combine path, signer, parent, command line, user, frequency, and network behavior.
Benign administrative activity can resemble attacker behavior, so analyst triage must consider expected software and role.

lessons.title: Windows, Linux, and Cloud Event Patterns
lessons.description: This lesson gives a cross-platform mental model for SOC analysts: authentication, process execution, privilege changes, service creation, configuration changes, and cloud administrative actions. It avoids platform-specific memorization and instead teaches event categories that map to investigations.
learningObjectives: Identify equivalent security event categories across operating systems and cloud platforms.
Build investigation questions that survive tool changes.
Explain why vendor IDs should be treated as implementation details.

items: Cross-platform categories include identity, process, persistence, privilege, network, configuration, and administrative change.
Vendor event IDs matter, but analyst reasoning should begin from the behavior being investigated.
Cloud environments require attention to API calls and identity context because traditional host/network visibility may be incomplete.

quiz.question: What is the best way to stay tool-independent?
options: Reason from behavior and investigation questions first
quiz.answer: Reason from behavior and investigation questions first
quiz.explanation: Behavior-oriented reasoning transfers across tools and platforms while vendor IDs remain implementation-specific.

summary: Cross-platform categories include identity, process, persistence, privilege, network, configuration, and administrative change.
Vendor event IDs matter, but analyst reasoning should begin from the behavior being investigated.
Cloud environments require attention to API calls and identity context because traditional host/network visibility may be incomplete.

tasks.title: Trace a Suspicious Web Session
tasks.description: Use a small set of network and endpoint events to reconstruct a suspicious web session.
tasks.problemStatement: A workstation generated a rare DNS lookup followed by a short outbound TLS session and a process tree showing an unexpected script host. Determine what can be concluded and what remains unknown.
objectives: Build a time-ordered timeline.
Separate facts from hypotheses.
List two additional data sources needed for confirmation.
requirements: The sample events in the task statement
tasks.hint: Do not jump from “rare” to “malicious.” Link DNS, process, and network observations by host and time.
tasks.solutionCode:
events = [
    {"t": "10:01:02", "kind": "dns", "host": "ws-17", "detail": "rare-domain.test"},
    {"t": "10:01:03", "kind": "process", "host": "ws-17", "detail": "script-host.exe spawned"},
    {"t": "10:01:05", "kind": "network", "host": "ws-17", "detail": "TLS -> 203.0.113.55:443"},
]
for event in sorted(events, key=lambda e: e["t"]):
    print(event["t"], event["kind"], event["detail"])

print("Need corroboration: endpoint command line/file reputation and network/proxy context.")
tasks.solutionExplanation: The timeline links multiple data sources but intentionally stops short of declaring compromise. Confirmation requires richer endpoint and network context.

modules.title: SIEM and Security Log Analysis
modules.description: Teach the SOC search workflow, SIEM pipeline concepts, KQL fundamentals, case context, and telemetry health.

lessons.title: SIEM Concepts: Ingest, Parse, Normalize, Search, Correlate
lessons.description: A SIEM is best understood as a pipeline and analysis environment rather than a magic detection engine. This lesson introduces ingestion, parsing, enrichment, indexing, normalization, search, correlation, alerting, and case management.
learningObjectives: Trace an event from source to analyst query.
Explain parsing and normalization failures.
Differentiate search, correlation, detection, and case management.

items: Pipeline stages create failure points: dropped events, parser errors, time shifts, field mapping errors, or delayed ingestion.
Normalization helps cross-source detection but must preserve source-specific evidence.
A detection rule is only as good as the data it can actually see.

quiz.question: Which stage converts raw source content into usable fields?
quiz.answer: Parsing/normalization
quiz.explanation: Parsing extracts structure and normalization aligns fields for analysis.

summary: Pipeline stages create failure points: dropped events, parser errors, time shifts, field mapping errors, or delayed ingestion.
Normalization helps cross-source detection but must preserve source-specific evidence.
A detection rule is only as good as the data it can actually see.

lessons.title: Search Strategy: Start With a Question
lessons.description: Efficient SOC queries are driven by investigative questions. This lesson shows how to start with one observable, add constraints gradually, inspect distributions, and pivot through identifiers such as user, host, IP, hash, process, or case ID.
learningObjectives: Turn an investigation question into a query sequence.
Use narrowing and expansion deliberately.
Choose pivot fields that support correlation.

items: A useful sequence is: establish scope → inspect frequency → isolate outliers → pivot to related entities → verify with independent evidence.
Avoid writing a huge query first; smaller staged queries are easier to validate and debug.
A good pivot has stable semantics: user, host, process, IP, hash, domain, or event/correlation ID.

quiz.question: What is a good first step before writing a complex SIEM query?
quiz.answer: Ask a precise investigation question
quiz.explanation: A concrete question keeps the query focused and reduces unnecessary complexity.

summary: A useful sequence is: establish scope → inspect frequency → isolate outliers → pivot to related entities → verify with independent evidence.
Avoid writing a huge query first; smaller staged queries are easier to validate and debug.
A good pivot has stable semantics: user, host, process, IP, hash, domain, or event/correlation ID.

resources.title: Microsoft Learn — KQL for Microsoft Sentinel

lessons.title: KQL Foundations for SOC Analysis
lessons.description: Kusto Query Language (KQL) is widely used in Microsoft Sentinel. This lesson introduces `where`, `project`, `summarize`, `extend`, `join`, and time filtering as transferable query concepts. The course treats KQL as one practical example of SIEM hunting rather than the only way to analyze logs.
learningObjectives: Write basic KQL filters and aggregations.
Summarize event counts by user or source address.
Explain when a join is useful for security analysis.

notes.text:
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where ResultType != 0
| summarize failures=count() by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
| top 20 by failures desc

items: `where` filters records; `summarize` aggregates; `project` selects fields; `extend` creates derived values; `join` combines related tables.
Use narrow time windows during investigation to reduce noise and improve query performance.

quiz.question: Which KQL operator groups records to calculate counts?
quiz.answer: summarize
quiz.explanation: `summarize` performs aggregations such as counts and distinct counts.

summary: `where` filters records; `summarize` aggregates; `project` selects fields; `extend` creates derived values; `join` combines related tables.
Use narrow time windows during investigation to reduce noise and improve query performance.

lessons.title: Dashboards, Cases, and Alert Context
lessons.description: A SOC dashboard is useful only when it helps decisions. This lesson covers alert enrichment, dashboards, bookmarks, case timelines, and analyst notes. The key principle is to preserve the evidence trail so another analyst can reproduce the reasoning.
learningObjectives: Define the minimum context an alert should display.
Explain how case notes improve repeatability.
Identify when a dashboard metric can mislead analysts.

items: Useful alert context includes the detection reason, entities, timestamps, data sources, relevant prior activity, and links to raw evidence.
Dashboards show aggregate trends but can hide long-tail anomalies if analysts only inspect top counts.

SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where ResultType != 0
| summarize failures=count() by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
| top 20 by failures desc

// Query 2: successful sign-in after failures
let failures = SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where ResultType != 0
| summarize firstFailure=min(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where ResultType == 0
| join kind=inner failures on UserPrincipalName, IPAddress
| where TimeGenerated > firstFailure

steps: Load the supplied JSONL events into a local Python program.

Identify any successful sign-in that follows a burst of failures.
Pivot on the affected user and host to inspect additional events.

practicals.solution:
import json
from collections import defaultdict
from datetime import datetime, timezone


def parse_ts(value):
    return datetime.fromisoformat(value.replace("Z", "+00:00")).astimezone(timezone.utc)

with open("events.jsonl", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    events = [json.loads(line) for line in fh if line.strip()]

failures = defaultdict(list)
for event in events:
    if event.get("event_type") == "authentication_failure":
        key = (event.get("user"), event.get("src_ip"))
        failures[key].append(event)

for key, items in failures.items():
    items.sort(key=lambda e: parse_ts(e["ts"]))
    print(key, len(items), items[0]["ts"], items[-1]["ts"])

# A production implementation would add window evaluation,
# success-after-failure correlation, device context, and case output.

This lesson introduces the data model and how analysts can read structured intelligence without requiring them to become STIX developers.
learningObjectives: Identify common STIX object categories.
Explain why relationships matter in threat intelligence.
Read a small STIX-like object and extract useful context.

items: STIX represents intelligence as objects and relationships; patterns can describe observables that may support detection.
STIX is a representation model, not a guarantee that every indicator is accurate.

quiz.answer: A way to express how threat-intelligence objects relate

lessons.title: TAXII for Threat-Intelligence Exchange
lessons.description: TAXII is a transport protocol for exchanging cyber threat information and can carry STIX content. This lesson covers collections, API concepts, authentication/authorization considerations, pagination, and why STIX and TAXII are independent standards.
learningObjectives: Explain the roles of STIX and TAXII.
Describe how a SOC might consume a threat-intelligence collection.
Identify operational risks such as stale feeds and excessive indicator volume.

items: STIX defines structure and semantics; TAXII defines a standardized way to exchange cyber threat information and can transport non-STIX data.
Feed integration needs provenance, confidence, freshness, deduplication, and safe matching logic.
Blindly importing every indicator can create noise and operational risk.

quiz.question: Which pairing is correct?
options: STIX is a transport protocol and TAXII is a malware family
STIX is a CTI representation and TAXII is an exchange protocol
TAXII is a firewall rule format
quiz.answer: STIX is a CTI representation and TAXII is an exchange protocol
quiz.explanation: STIX and TAXII are independent standards with complementary roles.

summary: STIX defines structure and semantics; TAXII defines a standardized way to exchange cyber threat information and can transport non-STIX data.
Feed integration needs provenance, confidence, freshness, deduplication, and safe matching logic.

tasks.title: Score and Operationalize Threat Indicators
tasks.description: Create an analyst-friendly workflow for deciding which threat indicators deserve matching in local telemetry.
tasks.problemStatement: The SOC receives a mixed feed of domains, IPs, and hashes with inconsistent freshness and confidence. Build a scoring approach that avoids blindly treating the feed as ground truth.
objectives: Define a minimum metadata model for indicators.
Score freshness, provenance, confidence, and local relevance.
Define actions for high-, medium-, and low-confidence indicators.
tasks.hint: Do not score only on reputation. Include age, provenance, confidence, and whether the indicator can be linked to local activity.
tasks.solutionCode:
def indicator_priority(confidence, age_days, local_hits, provenance_quality):
    score = 0
    score += 2 if confidence >= 80 else 1 if confidence >= 50 else 0
    score += 2 if age_days <= 7 else 1 if age_days <= 30 else 0
    score += 2 if local_hits > 0 else 0
    score += 2 if provenance_quality == "trusted" else 1 if provenance_quality == "known" else 0
    return score

print(indicator_priority(90, 3, 2, "trusted"))
tasks.solutionExplanation: This is a training model, not a universal scoring standard. The key is to preserve metadata and use a consistent decision rule so feeds improve investigation rather than overwhelm analysts.

lessons.title: Threat Hunting: Hypothesis Before Query
lessons.description: Threat hunting is a proactive investigation driven by a hypothesis about adversary behavior or a weakness in existing detection. This lesson teaches hypothesis formation, data requirements, hunt scope, and documenting outcomes.
learningObjectives: Form a testable hunting hypothesis.
Choose telemetry that can support or falsify the hypothesis.
Record hunt assumptions, results, and next actions.

items: A good hypothesis is falsifiable: it predicts observable behavior.
Start with a behavior, asset population, or technique—not with a random query.
A hunt should end in one of three useful states: no supporting evidence found, evidence found requiring investigation, or a detection/telemetry improvement identified.

options: It predicts observable behavior and can be supported or falsified

quiz.answer: It predicts observable behavior and can be supported or falsified
quiz.explanation: Hunting is most productive when the hypothesis drives observable tests.

summary: A good hypothesis is falsifiable: it predicts observable behavior.
Start with a behavior, asset population, or technique—not with a random query.

lessons.title: Hunting With Baselines and Outliers
lessons.description: SOC analysts use baselines to understand what is normal enough to make an anomaly worth investigating. This lesson covers prevalence, rarity, first-seen/last-seen concepts, seasonality, peer groups, and why anomaly signals require context.
learningObjectives: Define a baseline for a user, host, or service.
Identify useful outlier dimensions.
Avoid treating statistical rarity as maliciousness.

items: Useful baseline dimensions include process prevalence, authentication source patterns, destination domains, service accounts, and expected administrative activity.
Peer grouping can reduce noise: compare a host to similar hosts rather than to the entire environment.
Anomaly ≠ maliciousness; it is a prioritization signal.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a baseline?
options: To provide context for identifying meaningful deviations from expected behavior
quiz.answer: To provide context for identifying meaningful deviations from expected behavior
quiz.explanation: Baselines provide context and reduce noise, but deviations still require investigation.

summary: Useful baseline dimensions include process prevalence, authentication source patterns, destination domains, service accounts, and expected administrative activity.
Peer grouping can reduce noise: compare a host to similar hosts rather than to the entire environment.

lessons.title: Network Hunting With Zeek Logs
lessons.description: Zeek provides rich protocol metadata such as conn, DNS, HTTP, SSL, SSH, SMB, and other logs. This lesson shows how an analyst can hunt using combinations of connection, name-resolution, and application metadata rather than payload content.
learningObjectives: Interpret common Zeek log relationships.
Build a simple network-hunting pivot chain.
Explain what encrypted traffic prevents an analyst from seeing directly.

notes.text:
# Conceptual hunt chain
DNS query -> conn.log flow -> TLS metadata -> host/process context

items: Zeek's common logs include conn.log, dns.log, http.log, ssl.log, ssh.log, files.log and others.
Protocol metadata is strongest when linked to endpoint identity and time.

practicals.title: Hunt Zeek Connection Metadata
practicals.description: Filter a synthetic Zeek-style conn.log dataset to find rare outbound connections and pivot to DNS and process evidence.
steps: Prepare JSONL records with conn-like fields for source host, destination, service, bytes, and timestamps.
Calculate destination prevalence by host group.
Flag destinations seen by only one host.
Join flagged destinations to synthetic DNS and process events.
Write an analyst note explaining the confidence limits.
practicals.output: A list of low-prevalence connections that can be used as pivots. The student must validate rarity against business context and corroborating telemetry before escalating.

lessons.title: IDS Telemetry With Suricata EVE
lessons.description: Suricata's EVE output can emit alerts, anomalies, protocol records, file information, and metadata as JSON. This lesson teaches how to read EVE fields, correlate an alert with DNS/HTTP/TLS context, and validate whether a signature reflects a meaningful threat.

lessons.title: Basic Digital Forensics for SOC Analysts
lessons.description: SOC analysts may need to preserve volatile and non-volatile evidence for escalation. This lesson introduces memory versus disk evidence, process lists, open connections, file metadata, logs, and acquisition boundaries without replacing dedicated forensic procedures.
learningObjectives: Distinguish volatile from non-volatile evidence.
Identify high-value artifacts to preserve early.
Explain why acquisition procedures must be controlled and documented.

items: Volatile evidence can change when the system continues running; examples include live process state and active network connections.
Disk artifacts include files, persistence configuration, and historical logs.
The SOC should follow organizational forensic procedures and know when to hand off to specialists.

quiz.question: Which is an example of volatile evidence?
quiz.answer: A live process list
quiz.explanation: Live process state can change quickly and may disappear after shutdown or process termination.

summary: Volatile evidence can change when the system continues running; examples include live process state and active network connections.

lessons.title: Safe Automation for SOC Work
lessons.description: Automation reduces repetitive analyst effort when actions are deterministic and well bounded. This lesson covers enrichment, deduplication, notification, ticket creation, evidence collection, and approval gates. It emphasizes that automation should not silently make high-impact decisions without governance.
learningObjectives: Identify safe candidates for automation.
Add validation and approval gates to high-impact actions.
Design automation that is observable, reversible where possible, and auditable.

items: Good automation targets repetitive, low-risk, high-volume steps such as enrichment, tagging, deduplication, or evidence packaging.
High-impact actions such as account disablement or endpoint isolation should respect authorization and, where appropriate, human approval.
Automation itself needs monitoring, access control, secrets management, and failure handling.

quiz.question: Which is a good early automation target?
options: Automatic evidence enrichment and case tagging
quiz.answer: Automatic evidence enrichment and case tagging
quiz.explanation: Low-risk, deterministic enrichment is easier to validate and safer to automate.

summary: Good automation targets repetitive, low-risk, high-volume steps such as enrichment, tagging, deduplication, or evidence packaging.

tasks.title: Build a Hypothesis-Driven Hunt
tasks.description: Design and execute a synthetic threat hunt using network and endpoint telemetry.
tasks.problemStatement: Your team suspects that a rare external destination may be associated with script execution on a subset of workstations. Test the hypothesis with staged queries and produce a conclusion.
objectives: Define the hunt hypothesis and required evidence.
Use DNS, connection, and process data as pivots.
Record evidence for and against the hypothesis.
Propose either a new detection or a telemetry improvement.
tasks.hint: Start with the rare destination, enumerate affected hosts, then look for execution context rather than searching every log field at once.
tasks.solutionCode:
hypothesis = "Hosts resolving rare-domain.test may show unusual script execution soon afterward."

hunt_steps = [
    "find DNS events for rare-domain.test",
    "list affected hosts and time ranges",
    "correlate outbound connections",
    "pivot to process execution around the same time",
    "compare prevalence against peer hosts",
]
print(hypothesis)
for step in hunt_steps:
    print("-", step)
tasks.solutionExplanation: The hunt is structured as a falsifiable sequence. A strong conclusion explains whether the predicted behavior was observed, how many entities were involved, and what evidence is missing.

lessons.title: SIEM, EDR, IDS, NDR, SOAR, and Case Platforms
lessons.description: SOC technology names are often confused. This lesson distinguishes their operational roles: SIEM for broad log/event analysis, EDR for endpoint visibility and response, IDS/IPS for network detection/prevention, NDR for network behavior analytics, SOAR for orchestration, and case systems for workflow and evidence. The exact product boundary varies by vendor.
learningObjectives: Explain the primary role of common SOC technologies.
Describe how tools complement each other.
Avoid assuming a single platform provides complete visibility.

items: Technology categories overlap in modern platforms, so classify by capability rather than marketing labels.
A useful architecture links telemetry → analytics → alert → case → response → feedback.
Tool integration should preserve timestamps, entities, evidence provenance, and action audit trails.

practicals.title: Map a SOC Toolchain to Capabilities
practicals.description: Design a vendor-neutral SOC architecture showing how telemetry, detection, investigation, and response capabilities connect.
steps: List the key security use cases the SOC must support.
Assign each use case the minimum required telemetry sources.
Map those sources to collection, storage, and analysis capabilities.
Add detection and case-management stages.
Add response orchestration only where it provides a safe benefit.
Mark one failure mode for each major pipeline stage.
practicals.solution:
Use a diagram or text flow such as:

Endpoint / Identity / Network / Cloud / Application
            ↓
      Collection + Time
            ↓
     Parse / Normalize
            ↓
   Search / Detection / Hunt
            ↓
        Alert / Case
            ↓
 Investigation / Enrichment
            ↓
 Response / Recovery / Lessons

For each stage, document ownership and a health check.
practicals.output: A use-case-driven architecture with explicit telemetry dependencies, decision points, and health checks.

quiz.answer: Orchestrating and automating security workflows across tools

summary: Technology categories overlap in modern platforms, so classify by capability rather than marketing labels.

lessons.title: SOC Platform Selection and Data Architecture
lessons.description: A SOC should choose platforms based on use cases, data requirements, scale, skills, cost, integration, and operational constraints. project.name: SOC Incident Investigation and Detection Improvement Lab
project.description: A controlled, synthetic SOC lab in which a student ingests JSONL security events from identity, endpoint, network, and application sources; normalizes them; detects suspicious authentication and process/network correlations; investigates scope; maps observed behavior to MITRE ATT&CK; produces an incident case record; and proposes a concrete detection or telemetry improvement. The dataset is synthetic and does not require interaction with real victims, external targets, or production systems.
steps: Create a local Python 3.11+ environment using only the standard library.
Load the synthetic events.jsonl dataset and validate every non-empty line as JSON.
Normalize records to shared fields including timestamp, host, user, event_type, src_ip, dst_ip, process, parent_process, and domain.
Run the supplied authentication-burst and process-to-network correlation logic.
Build a time-ordered timeline around the first high-confidence finding and enumerate related entities.
Separate observed facts from hypotheses and record missing telemetry that would raise or lower confidence.
Map the observed behavior to one or more MITRE ATT&CK techniques and cite the evidence for each mapping.
Write a case disposition containing severity rationale, scope, authorized containment recommendation, recovery checks, and unresolved questions.
Generate a machine-readable report and review it for deterministic output.
Propose one detection improvement and one telemetry improvement, each with a validation method.
Run the included unit tests and verify the supplied report is reproducible.

files.rules/authentication_burst.yml:
title: Training Authentication Burst
description: Identify repeated authentication failures for a single identity/source pair within a short window.
logsource:
  category: authentication
detection:
  selection:
    event_type: authentication_failure
  condition: selection
level: medium
falsepositives:
  - Approved testing
  - Misconfigured automation

code.run:
python3 src/soc_mini_lab.py data/events.jsonl --report soc_report.json
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v

project.explanation: The architecture is intentionally local and synthetic: JSONL is the telemetry boundary, the Python standard library provides deterministic normalization and correlation, the rule file illustrates portable detection logic, and unit tests validate critical behaviors. The generated report separates observed evidence from a disposition template so the student must make the actual analyst decision. The project demonstrates the course end to end: telemetry quality, investigation pivots, behavioral detection, ATT&CK reasoning, response planning, documentation, and improvement.
